extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, and news consumers/citizens interested in journalistic principles
extracted.subtask_description: A set of core principles and standards that define what journalism should do and how journalists should work to produce trustworthy, democratic news. The page summarizes the book's enumerated 'elements' and related guidance for practicing and evaluating journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism's first obligation is to the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism’s first obligation is to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book frames truth as a practical, functional truth that journalism should pursue (not absolute/philosophical truth). The goal is to supply citizens with the information they need to be free and self-governing; journalism 'chases a truth that is actionable and functional' and must reliably report events so people can plan and act. (Quotes: 'Tujuan utama jurnalisme adalah menyampaikan kebenaran...' and 'provide people with the information they need to be free and self-governing.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Its first loyalty is to citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Its first loyalty is to citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should place the public (readers/listeners/viewers) above employers, advertisers, or other interests. The page emphasizes that good journalism 'fulfills a duty to citizens, rather than to "consumers" or to stockholders' and cites survey findings that journalists list 'making the reader/listener/viewer your first obligation' as a core value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Its essence is a discipline of verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Its essence is a discipline of verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is presented as the core of journalistic objectivity — the method (not a claim that the journalist is free from bias). Verification is likened to the scientific method: develop consistent methods for testing information and a transparent approach to evidence. The authors list explicit verification rules to prevent reporting from becoming interpretive fiction: 1) Never add anything that was not there. 2) Never deceive the audience. 3) Be as transparent as possible about your methods and motives. 4) Rely on your own original reporting. 5) Exercise humility. The book emphasizes that verification and rigorous methods distinguish journalists from entertainers or propagandists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioners must maintain independence from those they cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Its practitioners must maintain an independence from those they cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must avoid being 'in lockstep with factions or vested interests' and must guard against conflicts of interest (including corporate conflicts). Independence means reporting without being beholden to sources, politicians, or owners. The page includes critique that authors did not devote enough space to corporate conflicts of interest, highlighting it as an important practical threat to independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: It must serve as an independent monitor (watchdog) of power
rubrics_metrics.description: It must serve as an independent monitor of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism should act as a watchdog over those in power, investigating and reporting on actions and abuses so citizens can hold authorities accountable. This watchdog role is presented as a core democratic function of the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: It must provide a forum for public criticism and compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: It must provide a forum for public criticism and compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should offer spaces where public debate, criticism, and negotiation can occur — enabling civic discussion and collective problem-solving. The element emphasizes journalism's role in facilitating public discourse rather than silencing or merely entertaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: It must strive to make the significant interesting and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: It must strive to make the significant interesting and relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should present important issues in ways that engage the public so that significant matters capture attention and inform action. This speaks to storytelling, presentation, and editorial judgment that prioritize civic relevance over trivial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: It must keep the news comprehensive and proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: It must keep the news comprehensive and proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage should be thorough and proportionate to the significance of events, resisting the trend of turning news into entertainment or overemphasizing sensational items. The page warns against 'news becoming entertainment' and notes the need for balanced allocation of coverage across subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioners must be allowed to exercise their personal conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Its practitioners must be allowed to exercise their personal conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should be permitted to follow moral judgment and conscience in their work. The book treats conscience as a subtle but essential element: while journalists owe loyalty to citizens and must verify, they also need personal ethical autonomy. The authors discuss conscience's complexity and note that journalists commonly see their duty as to the public rather than to employers or parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and conscience as foundational, disqualifying failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification and conscience are so fundamental to journalism that forms of communication failing these standards should be disqualified from being called journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee/authors specify that two elements — verification and conscience — are overarching: if an information vehicle lacks verification and conscience, it should be considered entertainment or propaganda rather than journalism. This functions as a gatekeeping standard for what counts as legitimate journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion and investigative journalism acceptable if verifiable and transparent
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion journalism and investigative journalism are legitimate parts of the tradition so long as they maintain verifiable accuracy and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book argues opinion or advocacy journalism can be 'honest' if it remains committed to factual accuracy and discloses motives; loyalty to a cause (not to a person/party) can be compatible with journalistic truth, provided verification and transparency are preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens have rights and responsibilities regarding news
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens have rights and responsibilities when it comes to the news — increasingly so as they become producers and editors themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page (via a review summary) includes a tenth principle emphasizing that the public is not only a recipient but also an active participant in the news ecosystem; citizens must exercise responsibility (e.g., discerning accuracy) as they consume and produce news in the digital age.
